questions.question: Which parts of the key contract does spec 054 own, compared with 004 and 051?

options.label: 054 owns the domain (Recommended)
options.description: 054 states the function from an input string to a canonical key or a refusal, including step precedence, the store's root spellings, the alphabet and the backend profiles. PATH-002 to PATH-007 move into 054 with their IDs unchanged, as BK-456 stage two did, so their existing tests keep their marks. 004 keeps the RemotePath value object (PATH-001, PATH-008 to PATH-017), and its constructor links to 054. 051 keeps the tree, and its Layering paragraph points at 054 instead of 004.

options.label: 054 mints new KEY- IDs
options.description: Same split, but every clause gets a new KEY-NNN ID. PATH-002 to PATH-007 become [DEPRECATED] stubs pointing at 054, and the tests are re-marked. This means more churn and two IDs per fact during the change.

options.label: 054 adds only what is new
options.description: 004 keeps its normaliser and gains a step order. 054 states only the alphabet, the store root spellings and the backend profiles, and links to 004. This is the smallest change, but the key domain is split over two specs.

questions.question: Portable key set, and what happens to a key a backend cannot store (your points 2 and 3)?

options.label: Floor + declared refusals (Recommended)
options.description: The store refuses only what no wire can carry: NUL and lone surrogates, on every backend (so Memory changes too). Every backend must accept a stated portable floor: POSIX portable filename characters, segment and key byte bounds. A key outside the floor but inside the domain can be refused only with InvalidPath, under a profile 054 names (POSIX segment bytes, Windows-forbidden names, object-store key bytes), and with no observable change to the store. That last part is an outcome, not a requirement to check before I/O.

options.label: No floor, declared refusals
options.description: The domain is the same and refusals work the same way, but no set of keys is guaranteed on every backend. Simpler to state and test, but a caller cannot know which keys are portable.

options.label: Fixed alphabet everywhere
options.description: The store refuses anything outside a fixed portable alphabet and length bound, on every backend, before I/O. This is the most portable option, but it breaks existing keys that use spaces, non-ASCII characters or ':' on S3, Memory and others.

questions.question: How should root spellings at the store level relate to BE-029's root spellings at the backend level?

options.label: Two levels, store widens (Recommended)
options.description: At the store, every input that normalises to the empty key is the root. That includes '', '.', './', '/' and '//', plus '\' if backslash is still folded. Folder-shaped calls answer for the root and file-shaped calls refuse. BE-029 keeps its backend-level set, and 054 links to it. Today Store refuses './' and '/', so code breaks this clause: no mark yet, gap recorded under Rule 7.

options.label: Two levels, store stays narrow
options.description: At the store only '' and '.' are the root. Every other input that normalises to empty is InvalidPath on every call. This matches the code and the STORE-002 tests, but '/a' becomes 'a' while '/' is refused.

options.label: One rule, BE-029's six
options.description: The store root set is exactly BE-029's six slash-and-dot spellings. '\' and other inputs are refused, so the root has to be decided before the backslash fold. It agrees with RootPath.dfy, but the precedence becomes order-dependent.

questions.question: What should spec 054 say about backslash, which is folded to '/' today and so makes `a\b` unaddressable?

options.label: Keep the fold, state it (Recommended)
options.description: '\' folds to '/' as the first step, ahead of the '..' and NUL refusals in precedence, so 'a\..\b' is refused. This matches the code, the PATH-002 tests and migration.md ('A Store turns a backslash into / first'). 054 states that `a\b` is outside the store's addressable set, as 051 and BE-032 A.2 already say.

options.label: Refuse it
options.description: InvalidPath for any '\' at the store, the same rule as BE-030 on the kernel. This removes the silent alias of a\b onto a/b, but breaks callers who pass Windows-style paths. The code breaks the clause today, so the gap is recorded.

options.label: Pass it through as a name char
options.description: `a\b` becomes a one-segment name and addressable, and backends that cannot store it refuse under a profile. It conflicts with BE-030's kernel refusal, so 053 would have to change, which is outside this PR's scope.

Spec 054 names four refusal profiles but does not say how a backend declares one, which leaves an open question inside the spec (SPEC-DESIGN Ready 3). Where should spec 054 say a profile is declared?

options.label: In the backend's spec (Recommended)
options.description: KEY-008 says a backend declares its profiles and their limits in its own spec (008 S3, 012 Azure and so on), and that a backend whose spec declares none refuses nothing. This needs no code and is decidable now, and the conformance suite checks it per backend. It stretches Rule 5's 'capability or driver flag' to a declared statement in a spec. Moving the declaration into a runtime flag later is BK-469's choice.

options.label: A driver flag on the kernel
options.description: Profiles are a field the driver declares, like `namespace` or `parents`, and the kernel enforces them before I/O. This fits Rule 5 literally and suits D3 step 2, but backends not on the kernel have no declaration until they migrate. The spec names a flag that no code has yet (gap recorded under BK-469).

options.label: A capability per profile
options.description: Capabilities such as `KEY_NAME_BYTES` live in the CapabilitySet, readable through `Store.supports`. A caller can query them, but CapabilitySet carries no limits (255 versus 1024), so a limit needs a second channel. This is the heaviest change to CAP-001.

Two review rounds have now flagged the same conflict. Spec 054 declares profiles in the backend's spec, while SPEC-DESIGN Rule 5 says 'declared by a capability or a driver flag'. A Note in 054 justifies the exception, but the authority doc is unchanged. How should it be resolved?

options.label: Amend Rule 5 in this PR (Recommended)
options.description: Change Rule 5 to say 'declared by a capability, a driver flag, or the backend's own spec' and drop 054's exception Note. This is one sentence in an authority doc, inside this PR, and it touches SPEC-DESIGN.md, which the parallel BK-456 session reads but does not edit. It removes the conflict at its source.

options.label: Keep the Note, defer the amendment
options.description: Leave Rule 5 as it is and keep 054's Note as a registered exception. Rule 5 can be amended or the exception withdrawn later, but no reserved BK ID is left to track that, so it rides on BK-469's text. Reviews will keep flagging it until then.

options.label: Switch to a driver flag
options.description: Undo the earlier decision: profiles become a driver-declared field, which matches Rule 5 literally. The spec then names a flag that no code has yet (a gap under BK-469), and backends not on the kernel have no declaration.

questions.question: Spec 054 (KEY-008) has a backend declare its refusal profiles in its own spec, but SPEC-DESIGN.md Rule 5 says a profile is 'declared by a capability or a driver flag'. A note in 054 explains why it departs from that, but a note in one spec can't override the authority doc. How should it be resolved?

options.label: Amend Rule 5 in this PR (Recommended)
options.description: Rule 5 would read 'declared by a capability, a driver flag or the backend's own spec', with the reason added to ADR-0048's rationale (an Accepted ADR, so this means a new superseding or amending record, or keeping the rationale in SPEC-DESIGN only). 054's Note shrinks to a link. Process docs change in a spec PR, but the conflict closes where it started.

options.label: Separate process item
options.description: Keep 054 as it is and file a follow-up to amend Rule 5. My reserved IDs (BK-468, BK-469) are used up, so you or the dispatcher would hand out a new one. The conflict stays on master until that lands.

options.label: Revert KEY-008 to a driver flag
options.description: The profiles become a driver-declared field, as Rule 5 says. This reverses your earlier answer, and the spec would name a flag no code has yet (gap added to BK-469). Backends not on the kernel get no declaration until they migrate.

Spec 054 mixes rules on the key parameter (the function K) with rules on the resulting Key (floor, backend refusal). How should it be restructured?

options.label: One spec, two stated layers (Recommended)
options.description: The Overview states the store's verdict as a composition: K(s) on the parameter, then the backend's admission of the Key K(s). Part 1, 'The key function', holds PATH-002 to PATH-007 and KEY-001 to KEY-006. Part 2, 'Keys a backend admits', holds KEY-007 and KEY-008. Terms split into parameter terms and Key terms. Section IDs are unchanged, so no marks move.

options.label: Split into two specs
options.description: 054 becomes the key function only. KEY-007, KEY-008 and KEY-A-01 move to a new spec 055, 'Keys a backend admits', with IDs unchanged. Each spec gets one subject and links to the other. Costs a new spec number (check it is free with the parallel session) and another round of link retargets.

options.label: Keep it, clarify in prose
options.description: Keep the layout and add a sentence to the Overview saying that sections 1 to 6 are over the parameter and 7 to 8 over the Key. This is the smallest change, but the reader still separates the two by hand.

On Windows Local, a Key whose name ends in a space or a dot (`a/     `, `a `, `a.`) reaches another Key's entity: the parent, or the name without the trailing characters. Spec 054 lets a backend refuse such a name but does not require it. What should the spec say?

options.label: Faithful admission clause (Recommended)
options.description: New KEY-009 in Part 2: a Key a backend admits reaches its own entity, never another Key's, wherever the key alone decides that. A backend whose namespace rewrites a name must therefore refuse such Keys, which in practice means declaring `name-chars`. Aliasing that depends on state, such as case on case-insensitive systems, stays with spec 051 § Name equality. Windows Local breaks the clause today without measurement; I'd add that to BK-469 and leave KEY-009 allowlisted, since no Windows test exists here.

options.label: Store refuses everywhere
options.description: A Part 1 refusal on every backend for names ending in a space or `.`, and for whitespace-only names. This is portable and simple, but it breaks keys like `a.` and `x ` on S3 and Memory, where they are stored faithfully, and it narrows K for one platform's quirk.

options.label: Note only
options.description: Keep the clauses as they are and add a Note naming the Windows hazard, with `name-chars` as the remedy. Nothing would oblige a backend to act, so the silent aliasing stays legal.

questions.question: Linux, S3, Azure and Memory store `a/     ` and `a.` as their own Keys; Windows Local (and likely Graph) rewrites a name ending in a space or a dot, so the Key reaches its parent or another name. Spec 054 permits that backend to refuse such names but does not oblige it. What should the spec say?

A backend that rewrites names (Windows Local) must refuse these Keys by declaring `name-chars`; Linux and S3 keep storing them. Aliasing that depends on state, such as case on case-insensitive systems, stays with spec 051 § Name equality. Windows breaks the clause today without measurement; I'd add that to BK-469 and allowlist KEY-009.

options.description: A Part 1 refusal on every backend for names ending in a space or `.` and for whitespace-only names. Portable, but it takes away keys Linux, S3 and Memory store correctly (`a.`, `x `), narrowing K for one platform's quirk.

options.label: Note only
options.description: Keep the clauses, and add a Note naming the hazard and `name-chars` as the remedy. Silent aliasing on Windows stays legal.

options.description: Keep the clauses, and add a Note naming the hazard and `name-chars` as the remedy. Silent aliasing on Windows stays legal.
options.label: Note only

questions.question: Linux, S3, Azure and Memory store `a/     ` and `a.` as their own Keys; Windows Local (and likely Graph) rewrites a name ending in a space or a dot, so the Key reaches its parent or another name. Spec 054 permits that backend to refuse such names but does not oblige it. What should the spec say?
How should the conflict between SPEC-DESIGN Rule 5 (a profile is declared by a capability or a driver flag) and spec 054 (a backend declares its profiles in its own spec) be resolved?

options.label: Keep postponed
options.description: Leave it as it is: 054's Note records the departure, and the PR thread stays open. Reviewers will keep flagging KEY-008 until someone decides.

options.label: Amend Rule 5 to allow it
options.description: Rule 5 would read 'declared by a capability, a driver flag, or the backend's own spec'. That is a process-doc change in this PR, and it needs a rationale: the declaration can live in prose until a runtime declaration exists, and a test then takes it as a parameter. The conflict closes, at the cost of a weaker Rule 5.

options.label: Driver flag in 054 (Recommended)
options.description: KEY-008 names a declaration on the driver, e.g. `key_limits` with name bytes, key bytes, name chars and reserved names, which the kernel enforces before I/O. This matches Rule 5 and fixes BK-469's raw-error class at D3 step 2. No code has the flag yet (a gap under BK-469), and backends not on the kernel declare nothing until they migrate, so they must admit every Key, which Local on Linux already breaks.

options.label: Capability plus limits
options.description: Profile capabilities in CapabilitySet, readable through `Store.supports`, plus a second channel for the numeric limits. Callers can query them, but this means the heaviest change to CAP-001.

questions.question: Which layer enforces the key-limits declaration?

options.label: Store, from the Backend (Recommended)
options.description: Backend gains `key_limits` (a class default like CAPABILITIES, overridable per instance), and Store checks it before delegating. This covers every backend now, kernel or not, and the kernel forwards its driver's value. It is one more Store-side check (STORE-004 'adds no I/O logic' is not affected, as there is no I/O).

options.label: Kernel, from the driver
options.description: The driver declares it and the kernel checks it in BE-030's pipeline. This fits the kernel's ownership of key rules, but backends not on the kernel get nothing until they migrate (RFC-0017 D3), so Local's leak stays until step 5.

options.label: Both layers
options.description: The Store checks for backends not on the kernel, and the kernel checks for kernel classes called directly. Most complete, but two checks state one rule, which is the duplication BE-029 warns about.

questions.question: What does a declared profile mean?

options.label: Exact rule (Recommended)
options.description: A backend refuses exactly the Keys its declaration names and admits all others. This is testable in both directions, and KEY-009 becomes 'a stripping namespace declares portable_names'. A backend cannot be lenient beyond its declaration.

options.label: Licence (as now)
options.description: The declaration says what a backend may refuse; it may still store those keys. This is more flexible, but tests can only check one direction and outcomes stay variable inside the licence.

'Add that to CLAUDE.md': I read 'that' as the migration caveat. Backends may diverge from spec, store and kernel while they migrate, which is acceptable only while no release is planned, so BK-469 has to be fixed (or its backends migrated) before the next publish. Where should that rule live?

options.label: Release blocker item (Recommended)
options.description: File a BL- item under Release Blockers: 'spec 054 divergence (BK-469) must close before the next PyPI publish'. The release checklist already stops on any open BL-, so this is gated, not just remembered. It needs an ID outside my reservation (gen-backlogid says BL-12 is next), so you'd confirm it. CLAUDE.md stays unchanged, per its 'link, don't copy' principle.

options.label: CLAUDE.md principle
options.description: A general rule in CLAUDE.md: 'During a migration onto the kernel, legacy backends may diverge from spec; a release requires the divergence closed'. Every session sees it, but no gate checks it, and CLAUDE.md is loaded on every turn, which is a cost.

options.label: CONTRIBUTING release step
options.description: Add a step to CONTRIBUTING.md § Release: check that no spec-divergence item (BK-469 and similar) is open. It lives where releases are run, but it is a hand step.

questions.question: Portable names and segments as a regex, so a user can test portability themselves. How far should this PR go?

options.label: Regex in spec, utility later (Recommended)
options.description: Spec 054's Terms define the portable name by one regex (it is ASCII, so bytes equal characters) and a portable floor Key by names joined with `/`, at most 255 bytes, with the prose kept as a gloss of the same definition. A public helper such as `remote_store.is_portable_key(key)` becomes a backlog item with its own spec section and tests, since this PR has no code (an ID from you).

options.label: Regex and helper now
options.description: Add the regex and a public `is_portable_key()` with a spec section, tests and docs in this PR. This is a new public API in a spec PR, and it widens the scope you set (no code fix).

options.label: Regex only, no helper
options.description: Add the regex to spec 054's Terms and decide nothing about tooling. Users copy the regex.

My reservation (BK-468, BK-469) is used up; across pushed branches the next safe BK is BK-472, but the paused BK-456 session mints from BK-470 upwards and may hold unpushed ones. Which ID?

options.label: BK-480 (Recommended)
options.description: Leaves a gap above the parallel session's range (BK-470 onwards), so a collision is very unlikely. `gen-backlogid` accepts gaps. I would tell that session.

options.label: BK-472
options.description: The next safe ID across pushed branches right now. It collides if the paused session has minted BK-472 locally and not pushed it yet.

options.label: Fold into BK-469
options.description: No new ID: BK-469 gains a sub-bullet for the helper. But its fix surface (backend breakages) differs from the helper's (new public API), and the backlog granularity rule says such surfaces stay separate.

options.label: Not now
options.description: File nothing. The idea stays in this conversation and the PR thread only.

How should the Windows behaviour behind KEY-009 (a trailing dot removed from every name, trailing spaces from the last) be measured on CI's windows-latest runner?

options.label: Strict xfail in the test (Recommended)
options.description: Mark the KEY-009 test `os_sensitive` and, on win32 Local, `xfail(strict=True, reason=BK-469)` instead of skip. CI then measures it on every run. If Windows aliases as documented, the cell shows XFAIL; if it does not, XPASS fails the job and tells us the Note is wrong. The breakage stays visible and nothing is hidden.

options.label: One-off probe workflow
options.description: A `workflow_dispatch` job runs `sdd/research/bk-468-key-probe/` scripts (extended with the trailing-dot cases and BUG-334's names) on windows-latest and uploads the output. It measures more cases at once, but it adds a workflow, runs once, and its result has to be copied into the trace by hand.

options.label: Leave it unmeasured
options.description: Keep the skip. The Windows claim stays documented and unmeasured until BK-469 or Local's migration step.
